grossMargin.name: Gross Margin
grossMargin.question: How much value remains after direct cost?
grossMargin.help: Of every $100 you sell, how much is left after paying what it costs to make or buy what you sold. At 40%, $40 of every $100 remains for expenses, debt, and profit.

ebitdaMargin.name: EBITDA Margin
ebitdaMargin.question: Are we profitable at the operating level?
ebitdaMargin.help: Of every $100 you sell, how much is left after day-to-day costs and expenses, before interest, tax, and asset wear (that is EBITDA). Higher is usually better: you have more room to maneuver.

netMargin.name: Net Margin
netMargin.question: How much final profit does each sale leave?
netMargin.help: Of every $100 you sell, how much is left at the end after costs, expenses, interest, and tax. At 8%, you keep $8. Higher is better; low or negative means little profit—or a loss.

nopatMargin.name: NOPAT Margin
nopatMargin.question: Does operations create profit after tax?
nopatMargin.help: Of every $100 you sell, how much profit the core business leaves after tax, as if there were no debt (NOPAT). Higher is better: operations themselves are creating more value.

operatingMargin.name: Operating Margin
operatingMargin.question: How profitable is the core business?
operatingMargin.help: Of every $100 you sell, how much the core business keeps after costs and expenses, before interest and tax. At 15%, $15 remains. Higher is better: everyday operations are more profitable.

ocfMargin.name: Operating Cash Flow (OCF) Margin
ocfMargin.question: Do sales convert into operating cash?
ocfMargin.help: Of every $100 you sell, how much actually lands in the bank from operations (operating cash flow). At 12%, $12 comes in. Higher is better; if it is low, sales look fine on paper but cash is slow.

fcfMargin.name: Free Cash Flow (FCF) Margin
fcfMargin.question: How much free cash does each peso sold generate?
fcfMargin.help: Of every $100 you sell, how much cash is left after running the business and investing in equipment or upgrades (free cash flow). At 6%, $6 is left. Higher is better: cash for debt, reserves, or owners.

effectiveTaxRate.name: Effective Tax Rate
effectiveTaxRate.question: What share of profit goes to tax?
effectiveTaxRate.help: Of every $100 of profit before tax, how much goes to taxes. At 30%, you pay $30. It is not “good or bad” by itself—compare it with prior periods and with what you expected to pay.

roic.name: ROIC (Return on Invested Capital)
roic.question: Is invested capital creating value?
roic.help: How much you earn after tax for every $100 invested in operations (invested capital: owners’ and lenders’ money put to work). At 15%, you earn $15. Higher is better if it beats the cost of that money.

roce.name: ROCE (Return on Capital Employed)
roce.question: What return does employed capital produce?
roce.help: How much the business produces for every $100 of capital employed (assets minus short-term debts). At 18%, they produce $18. Higher is better: you use what you have more effectively to generate operating profit.

roe.name: ROE (Return on Equity)
roe.question: What return do shareholders earn?
roe.help: How much owners earn for every $100 of their capital in the company. At 20%, they earn $20. Higher is usually better, but if it rises only because of heavy debt, risk is rising too.

roa.name: ROA (Return on Assets)
roa.question: How productive are our assets?
roa.help: How much net profit each $100 of everything the company owns produces (cash, customers, inventory, equipment). At 8%, they produce $8. Higher is better: your resources work harder.

gmroi.name: GMROI (Gross Margin Return on Inventory)
gmroi.question: Does inventory produce enough margin?
gmroi.help: How much gross margin (sales minus the cost of what you sold) each $100 tied up in inventory produces. At 200%, each $100 in stock leaves $200 of margin. Higher is better: inventory is working, not sitting.

ronic.name: RONIC (Return on New Invested Capital)
ronic.question: Does new capital generate attractive returns?
ronic.help: When you invest new money, how much extra after-tax profit it earns. At 12%, each new $100 leaves $12 more. Higher is better: the growth is worth the extra capital.

cashRoic.name: Cash ROIC
cashRoic.question: What cash return does invested capital produce?
cashRoic.help: How much operating cash comes in for every $100 of invested capital (money put to work). At 10%, $10 of cash comes in. Higher is better: capital shows up in the bank, not only on the income statement.

assetTurnover.name: Asset Turnover
assetTurnover.question: How much sales does each peso of assets produce?
assetTurnover.help: How many times a year your assets “turn” into sales. At 1.5, each $100 of assets generates $150 of sales. Higher is better: you use what you own more effectively to sell.

receivablesTurnover.name: Receivables Turnover
receivablesTurnover.question: How quickly do we convert receivables into sales?
receivablesTurnover.help: How many times a year you collect what customers owe you. At 12, you collect about 12 times a year (roughly monthly). Higher is better: sales cash comes back faster.

inventoryTurnover.name: Inventory Turnover
inventoryTurnover.question: How quickly does inventory turn?
inventoryTurnover.help: How many times a year you sell and restock inventory. At 6, you turn stock six times a year. Higher is usually better (less idle product), unless you stock out and lose sales.

payablesTurnover.name: Payables Turnover
payablesTurnover.question: How often do we refresh accounts payable?
payablesTurnover.help: How many times a year you pay suppliers. A lower number means you take longer to pay and keep cash longer. Avoid extremes: paying very late hurts the relationship; paying very early squeezes cash.

icTurnover.name: Invested Capital Turnover
icTurnover.question: How efficient is invested capital?
icTurnover.help: How much sales each $100 of invested capital generates (owners’ and lenders’ money in the business). At 2, those $100 generate $200 of sales. Higher is better: capital produces more volume.

nwcOfRevenue.name: NWC to Revenue
nwcOfRevenue.question: How much working capital does each sale require?
nwcOfRevenue.help: Of every $100 you sell, how much stays tied up in day-to-day operations (customers + inventory − suppliers). At 20%, you need $20. Lower is usually better: you sell without locking up as much cash.

capexOfRevenue.name: CapEx to Revenue
capexOfRevenue.question: How much do we reinvest in productive assets?
capexOfRevenue.help: Of every $100 you sell, how much you reinvest in equipment, facilities, or systems (CapEx). At 8%, that is $8. A healthy level covers wear and growth; too high squeezes cash, too low can leave the business aging.

sgaOfRevenue.name: OpEx to Revenue
sgaOfRevenue.question: How heavy are administrative expenses?
sgaOfRevenue.help: Of every $100 you sell, how much goes to admin, selling, and office costs. At 25%, that is $25. Lower is usually better, as long as you are not cutting what actually supports sales.

daOfRevenue.name: D&A to Revenue
daOfRevenue.question: How heavy is depreciation in sales?
daOfRevenue.help: Of every $100 you sell, how much is the accounting wear of equipment and intangibles (depreciation and amortization). At 5%, that is $5. A high % can mean heavy assets or weak sales.

currentRatio.name: Current Ratio
currentRatio.question: Can we cover short-term obligations?
currentRatio.help: If you owe $100 in the next 12 months, how much you have in assets that also turn into cash soon (cash, customers, inventory). 1.5 means $150. Above 1 is usually more comfortable; very low flags payment stress.

quickRatio.name: Quick Ratio
quickRatio.question: Can we pay without relying on inventory?
quickRatio.help: Like the current ratio, but without inventory. If you owe $100 soon, how much do cash and customer receivables cover? Around 1 or more is safer: you can pay without rushing to sell stock.

cashRatio.name: Cash Ratio
cashRatio.question: How much short-term debt does cash cover?
cashRatio.help: Of every $100 you owe in the short term, how much you already have in cash. At 0.3, you have $30. Higher gives more immediate safety; too high can mean cash sitting idle.

cashRunwayMonths.name: Months of breathing room
cashRunwayMonths.question: How many months can we operate with current cash?
cashRunwayMonths.help: With today’s cash and the current spending pace, how many months you could keep operating. More months mean a bigger cushion. Few months mean you depend on collecting soon or on new financing.

cashEfficiency.name: Cash Efficiency
cashEfficiency.question: Does EBITDA convert into free cash flow?
cashEfficiency.help: Of every $100 of EBITDA (operating profit before interest, tax, and asset wear), how much becomes free cash. At 70%, $70 reaches the bank. Higher is better: profit shows up as cash.

ccc.name: Cash Conversion Cycle (CCC)
ccc.question: How long does cash take to return to the business?
ccc.help: How many days your cash takes to complete the loop: from paying for inventory until the customer pays you, minus how long you take to pay suppliers. Fewer days is better: money returns faster.

dso.name: Average collection days (DSO)
dso.question: How many days do customers take to pay?
dso.help: On average, how many days customers take to pay you. At 45, you collect in about a month and a half. Lower is usually better: cash arrives sooner. If it rises, you are funding customers with your own cash.

dpo.name: Days Payable Outstanding (DPO)
dpo.question: How many days do we take to pay suppliers?
dpo.help: On average, how many days you take to pay suppliers. More days keep cash in your account, but stretching too far can hurt credit and deliveries. The healthy point is what you agreed, without overextending.

dio.name: Days Inventory Outstanding (DIO)
dio.question: How many days does inventory stay on hand?
dio.help: On average, how many days product sits in the warehouse before it sells. Fewer days is usually better (less cash sitting still), unless you run out of goods. If it rises a lot, inventory is piling up.

interestCoverage.name: Interest Coverage
interestCoverage.question: Does operations comfortably cover interest?
interestCoverage.help: How many times operating profit covers interest on debt. At 5, you earn five times what you pay in interest. Higher is better; near 1 or below means debt is weighing too heavily.

netDebtToEbitda.name: Net Debt to EBITDA
netDebtToEbitda.question: How many years of EBITDA is net debt?
netDebtToEbitda.help: How many years of EBITDA (operating profit before interest, tax, and asset wear) you would need to pay net debt (debt minus cash). At 2, about two years. Lower is more comfortable; very high means heavy debt.

financialLeverage.name: Financial Leverage
financialLeverage.question: How much assets support each peso of equity?
financialLeverage.help: For every $100 of owners’ capital, how many assets there are in total. At 3, there are $300 of assets (the rest is usually debt). Higher boosts upside and also risk if sales slip.

liabilityRatio.name: Liability Ratio
liabilityRatio.question: What share of assets is funded by liabilities?
liabilityRatio.help: Of every $100 in assets, how much is funded by debts and other obligations, not by owners’ money. At 60%, $60 belongs to third parties. Lower is usually more conservative; very high raises risk.

debtRatio.name: Debt Ratio
debtRatio.question: What share of assets uses interest-bearing debt?
debtRatio.help: Of every $100 in assets, how much is funded with interest-bearing debt. At 40%, $40. Lower is usually safer. This is not all liabilities—only debt that has a cost.

costOfDebt.name: Cost of Debt
costOfDebt.question: What is the effective cost of our debt?
costOfDebt.help: What borrowed money costs you, as a percentage. At 12%, you pay about $12 a year for every $100 of debt. Lower is better: financing is cheaper.

operatingLeverage.name: Operating Leverage
operatingLeverage.question: How sensitive is profit to sales?
operatingLeverage.help: If sales rise or fall 10%, how much operating profit moves. A high number means you gain more on the way up and suffer more on the way down. Understand it; don’t maximize it blindly.

debtToRevenue.name: Debt to Revenue
debtToRevenue.question: What share of sales does debt represent?
debtToRevenue.help: How much debt you have compared with what you sell in the period. At 50%, debt equals half of your sales. Lower is usually easier to service; very high means sales barely support the debt.

keyScore.name: Key Score
keyScore.question: What is the overall financial health of the business?
keyScore.help: A score that summarizes business health by combining gross margin, EBITDA margin, owners’ return, and the ability to pay short-term bills. Higher is better: several fronts are healthy at once, not just one.

valueDriver.name: Value Driver
valueDriver.question: Does sales growth drive EBITDA?
valueDriver.help: When sales grow, how much of that extra turns into more EBITDA (operating profit before interest, tax, and asset wear). If EBITDA keeps up, the growth is worth it. If not, you are growing without earning more.

revenueGrowth.name: Revenue Growth
revenueGrowth.question: How fast is revenue growing?
revenueGrowth.help: How much sales rose or fell versus the comparable period. At +10%, you sell 10% more. Growth is good if you also protect margin and cash; a sustained drop calls for a look at prices, volume, or customers.

ebitdaGrowth.name: EBITDA Growth
ebitdaGrowth.question: How fast is EBITDA growing?
ebitdaGrowth.help: How much EBITDA—operating profit before interest, tax, and asset wear—rose or fell versus the comparable period. Rising faster than sales is usually healthy; falling while you sell more flags cost pressure.

wacc.name: WACC (Weighted Average Cost of Capital)
wacc.question: What is the minimum return we must beat?
wacc.help: The average cost of the business’s money: what owners and lenders “charge” together (WACC). At 11%, you should earn more than 11% on invested capital. Lower makes it easier to create value; it is your minimum bar.

costOfEquity.name: Cost of Equity
costOfEquity.question: What return do shareholders expect?
costOfEquity.help: The return owners expect for risking their money. At 14%, they want about $14 a year per $100. It is not a cash expense, but if ROE sits below it, shareholders are not being compensated.

economicSpread.name: Economic Spread
economicSpread.question: Does ROIC exceed our cost of capital?
economicSpread.help: The gap between what invested capital earns (ROIC) and what that capital costs (WACC). At +3%, you earn 3 points above the minimum. Positive creates value; negative means you earn less than it costs to fund the business.

shareholderMargin.name: Shareholder Margin
shareholderMargin.question: Does shareholder return exceed its cost?
shareholderMargin.help: The gap between what owners earn (ROE) and what they expect to earn. At +4%, the shareholder gets 4 extra points. Positive is favorable; negative means the return does not cover the risk they take.

dividendPayout.name: Dividend Payout
dividendPayout.question: What share of profit is distributed?
dividendPayout.help: Of every $100 of net profit, how much is paid out to owners as dividends. At 30%, $30 leaves and $70 stays in the company. Neither high nor low is always better: it depends on whether the business needs that cash.
